items.title: Satisfactory: The Board Game Preview
items.content_text: Automation and factory-building games have become pretty popular over the past few years, with Coffee Stain Studios' Satisfactory being one of the stars of the genre. I have always admired the sprawling conveyor belts and mega structures of the factory-building powerhouse from a comfortable distance, dipping my toe into the waters with messy (but kind of functional) factories of my own. Soon, factory builders will have a whole new way to build out their process, as Mood Publishing, the same publisher behind Hitman: The Board Game , is looking to bring the beloved factory sim to your tabletop with Satisfactory: The Board Game and the launch of their latest crowdfunding campaign over on Gamefound . We were sent an early prototype copy to check out, in addition to playing a demo with the game’s designer, David Thor Fjalarsson, to see if a tabletop game can capture and refine the Satisfactory experience down to the size of a kitchen table-sized factory. In Satisfactory: The Board Game (referred to simply as "Satisfactory" going forward), designed by David Thor Fjalarsson, up to four players will have to mine, refine, and upgrade their factories in an effort to earn the most FICSIT points before the space elevator is finished. The turns themselves are surprisingly straightforward; on your turn, you will perform two actions, either build something, move around the map, or have your factory do its work. Once each player has taken their turn, the production phase occurs, where everyone's mines will activate, drilling for one of the three basic materials—limestone, iron, or copper—and existing materials will move down their conveyors towards getting refined into better resources. Then, the whole cycle repeats itself. Even in my first game, by the time my group had reached the second or third round, we had the flow down. The game itself takes place on a large hex-grid representation of the video game's massive world, with random creatures and biomes that get placed during setup, along with various material-rich points where mines can be placed. The “Move” action is pretty self-explanatory, allowing you to move your piece up to a number of spaces equal to your movement value, with some spaces that can only be crossed once certain technologies or vehicles have been built. Landing on a point can grant you resources, or allow you to claim one of the tokens mentioned earlier. If you prefer to get some extra work in at your factories, you can instead opt for the “Workshop” action, which lets you either move a beltline of resources down a spot or refine a single block of material into a higher-tier version, which is a crucial component for when you build. "Stringing together these bonuses to create some wild turns was some of the most fun I had playing Satisfactory. Speaking of building things, the “Build” action was my favorite, and what I would consider the core thing to do in this game. At any time, players will have access to build their staple devices—extractors, refineries, et cetera—in addition to a random pool of cards of varying tiers that get unlocked over the course of the game. These cards, like the Jet Pack to help you get around quicker or weapons to tackle the wildlife, are a great help, but the main structures you can construct have an added little treat to them. Depending on what you build, you will have a bonus action that you can take, determined by what you have built. Building a miner, for instance, will allow you to immediately build a Belt, which will then trigger the Belt’s bonus, giving you a free movement action, or the Constructor, giving you an extra action you can take on your turn. Stringing together these bonuses to create some wild turns was some of the most fun I had playing Satisfactory. When it comes to playing, Satisfactory's tabletop adaptation has opted for a competitive “race for points” experience for its main game, instead of the cooperative focus from the PC title — though the promised final game will include a co-op and solo modes as well. That said, don't expect to be bombing or taking out the other players' extractors and belts with some cardboard corporate terrorism within the game. Instead, once a player has claimed a tile by building something on it, no other player can develop on it, though they can still cross over with no issue. Satisfactory can still be “mean,” but it’s more like cleverly getting in the way or making expansion for your opponents annoying as opposed to turning the planet into a battlefield. This sort of headbutting really only comes out when you start getting to the three- or four-player counts. At two players, because both players have so much more space, I was surprised and impressed with how different Satisfactory manages to feel. During my two-player game, with far less worry about my factory getting locked in by other players, I instead was able to focus and work out how best I wanted to try and optimize (as optimized as you could get in a game like this after only a couple plays) my system. It honestly felt like I was playing different games based on the player counts, with two players focusing on optimizing and planning out turns to maximize earning points, while with three, and especially four, figuring out how best to expand my factory and balancing blocking resources from the others was much more in the forefront of my mind. Oddly enough, I think I actually enjoyed the puzzley nature of the lower player count more, as both of us weren’t forced into conflict with one another, and I could better test out what Satisfactory offers. In one two-player game, I focused on maxing out my basic resource production, getting all of my extractors online as fast as I could, and expanding my reach to a few farther-out “rich” tiles, which further let me produce more of the resource during production phases. Having an almost overabundance of these cheaper resources allowed me to quickly gobble up and complete the early-game Milestones, netting me a bunch of points and rocketing me out into the lead, faster than the elevator could take me. During one particularly memorable event, thanks to the rewards given by completing the goals and what I had earned from various Biomes I visited that turn, I was able to complete four of the Milestones back -to-back-to-back. It was a straight dopamine shot to the system, and basically sold me on Satisfactory alone. I, admittedly, approached Satisfactory from the viewpoint of someone who hasn’t sunk all that many hours into the game that it has been adapted from, but even this condensed package still manages to FEEL like Satisfactory. Watching my pathways of conveyor belts expand outwards across the map, discovering alternate recipes, and building the network of machines to allow me to continue to refine my goods and open up new technologies is still all here. Even memorable critters like Bean are here. There are plenty of other nods that longtime players will pick up on better than I, but I applaud the designers for still managing to make this feel like Satisfactory at its heart. The tabletop adaptation obviously can’t replicate the massive, near-limitless scale of the PC game, but it looks to have successfully mined what matters most: building an efficient system and then riding it until you need to upgrade it to reach loftier heights. If there is one thing that interested builders should be aware of, it is that Satisfactory is not a small game. It requires a good bit of table space to play, and it will assault you with icons. When its multiple boards, piles of cards, large play board, and resource tokens are all laid out, this is a surprisingly imposing tabletop experience. Some smart decisions, such as keeping the material types down to just three, do help keep you from being overwhelmed by resource management, thankfully. Frankly, keeping track of and remembering what all the icons meant was more of a hassle than managing my stockpiles of colored cubes. Different icons appear all over the place, on cards, on the map, the player boards, and even the victory point track, and at least in the prototype I had, it did not come with a player reference card. Thankfully, I’ve been assured there is one that will come with the release copy, which should alleviate some of that headache of keeping track of what means what. It took the better part of the game to grasp the icons, but by the end, it did start clicking, and again, much of that pain will be lessened with the inclusion of a reference card. Satisfactory: The Board Game is still being tweaked and adjusted, but Mood appears to have succeeded in shrinking down the complex factory-building game and distilling it down to its raw materials to create a surprisingly approachable (if not a bit intimidating-looking) board game. The limited action choices you have on your turn help keep turns quick and snappy, but I can certainly see how, if you have a tendency to hyper-analyze your turns or have to make the most optimized play, turns could easily take a bit longer. Regardless, the implementation here, adapting so many systems while still being a game that doesn’t take all day to play (my games usually lasted 2 - 3.5 hours), is impressive. Thankfully, before backing the game, a draft version of the rules has been posted along with the full list of add-ons and what is included in the pledge tiers over on the Gamefound page . Or, better yet, you and your game group can try it for yourselves in Tabletop Simulator on Steam using an official preview build mod made by MOOD! Now, back to trying to figure out how to build my own mega factory.
items.title_en: Satisfactory: The Board Game Preview

items.title: Greta Gerwig's Narnia: The Magician's Nephew Wins Over Skeptical Fans With First Poster
items.excerpt: The first poster for Greta Gerwig's Narnia: The Magician's Nephew is here, and it seems to have won over a few of the more skeptical fans.
items.content_text: The first poster for Greta Gerwig's Narnia: The Magician's Nephew is here, and it seems to have won over a few of the more skeptical fans. Netflix shared an ethereal glimpse at the new Narnia movie on social media today. It came with the promise that a first look at the Barbie director's foray into the beloved fantasy universe will arrive via trailer tomorrow, though specifically when it will premiere is unclear. The Narnia: The Magician's Nephew poster (below) seems to call back to art featured on some copies of author C. S. Lewis' original The Magician's Nephew novels. That would mean the three individuals illuminated by iridescent light here are Polly (Beatrice Campbell), Digory (David McKenna), and their flying horse, Fledge. The spacey lion gracing the background, meanwhile, teases Meryl Streep's Aslan. The new poster for Gerwig's Netflix movie doesn't reveal much about its story or characters, but it's the look and feel that has fans taken aback. Even some of the more skeptical viewers, who have feared what an adaptation of Lewis' work would look like in 2026, like what they see here, with many taking to social media to praise the art. "Well, that actually looks pretty awesome," one Reddit user said . "Credit where credit is due, that is one hell of a poster," another added . "It looks like a poster from a 1980s/early 1990s fantasy film and I am here for it," another user added . That's not to say that there aren't still those who have yet to be impressed. Most of the concern seems to come from a place of dread that some of the most revered characters in fantasy could be warped or damaged on impact. Some naysayers are more vocal than others, but in reality, it's hard to say if Gerwig will land the plane just yet, but we'll definitely have a better idea when the film premieres next year. "If I knew nooooothing else about this movie, I'd be excited," one of the more cautious fans said . "I really like a lot of the visual stuff they’re doing with the movie," another explained . "Lots of cool filmic feeling stuff especially here. I just don’t like the time jump and the costume for Jadis doesn’t feel regal. It should be good technically but less so in other places." In a relatively unlikely move from Netflix, Narnia: The Magician's Nephew is set to first come to theaters via IMAX sneak previews starting February 10, 2027. It will then receive a global wide release February 12, with streaming subscribers then able to watch from the comfort of their homes starting April 2. Also included in the film's cast are Carey Mulligan, Daniel Craig, Emma Mackey, and Ciarán Hinds. While we wait to see how the movie may stray from the source material, you can check out more early details here . You can also check out what we learned after its logo reveal .

items.title: Will You Get a Paramount+ Subscription to Watch Avatar: Seven Havens?
items.content_text: Avatar: Seven Havens premiered last week, exclusively on Paramount+. And shortly after that happened, Paramount went ahead and revealed that seasons 3 and 4 of the series are already greenlit alongside another Avatar project. As someone who doesn't currently have a Paramount+ subscription , I find myself conflicted. Avatar: The Last Air Bender is my favorite animated show of all time and I loved what the creators did with The Legend of Korra as well. So while I really want to watch Seven Havens, I don't really want to add a Paramount+ subscription to my monthly streaming bill. I could have easily written off the new show as a shameless grab for my subscription dollars, but the very positive reviews of the premiere make it it harder to avoid. Pair that with the fact that I still haven't seen the Avatar Aang movie yet, and it seems inevitable that I'm going to get at least a temporary subscription just to watch those two things. The good news is that the release schedule for Avatar: Seven Havens is actually pretty condensed. There are 13 episodes in season 1, but they are all releasing in batches. The final four episodes are currently set to be added to the service on October 30. So if you sign up for a one-month subscription now, you should be able to finish the series before you cancel. Paramount+ used to offer a free trial, but they decided to drop that at the beginning of the year when they began adding UFC fights to the platform. That being said, there is a free trial of sorts available if you choose to take the Walmart+ route. If you haven't used it already, you can currently sign up for 30 days for $1, which happens to include access to basic Paramount+ subscription. With the Paramount Skydance acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery now complete , this is likely not the last time a Paramount+ subscription will be needed to watch a popular show. For now I'm still clinging to my HBO Max, Hulu, and Disney+ bundle as my main source of content, but who knows when that could go away. For now I'm glad I only have to spend an extra $8.99 to watch the new Avatar show.
items.title_en: Will You Get a Paramount+ Subscription to Watch Avatar: Seven Havens?

items.content_text: The foldable Apple iPhone Duo is real and it’s almost here. The iPhone Duo tops both of the other recently-released iPhones with its own scary, $1,999 price tag. That’s $100 more than the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 that launched earlier this year. Then again, specs-wise, it’s probably more comparable to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra , which costs $2,099 out of the gate. Either way, you’re going to want to protect it. The big open question is going to be what’s the best way to protect the iPhone Duo. Case makers have had plenty of practice with foldables from Samsung and Google, but it’ll still be a little riskier to pick something for Apple’s phone, as it’s a brand new device in what is a slightly unusual, passport-style form factor (or would be, if Samsung hadn’t beat Apple to the punch in July ). The case makers I’ve chosen below are historically good at what they do, but mainly, I’d recommend going with an Apple-made option over all of them, at least until third-parties have had a chance to work out any kinks with their designs. Apple iPhone Duo Case Best iPhone Duo Case Apple’s first-party iPhone Duo case comes in Navy Blue and Sand, complementing the two Duo options – black or white – the company is offering its new foldable in. It’s got MagSafe support (it should also work with a 25W Qi2 charger), a matte coating) and is made of a polycarbonate material with a matte coating. Being a first-party Apple case, it’s guaranteed to fit an iPhone Duo, which isn’t something I’d necessarily expect out of a third-party option this early in the game. You can get the Apple iPhone Duo Case straight from the Apple Store now, for $79. Apple Duo Folio with Kickstand Best iPhone Duo Kickstand Case The Apple iPhone Duo Folio with Kickstand isn’t a case as much as it is a magnetic cover, very similar to the ones the company has made for iPads for years. The Duo Folio doesn’t cover the sides of the phone, and it totally covers the outer display when you’re not using it. Based on Apple’s product imagery, you can flop the outer display part of the cover off to use it, but it’s not clear if it then folds behind the phone, as it does on iPad folio cases. The iPhone Duo Folio with Kickstand comes in Navy Blue and Taupe, both with the same textured fabric found on the iPhone 18 Pro’s TechWoven cases. It’s also spendy, at $129. That’s a full $50 more than, say, Apple’s Smart Folio for iPad Pro 11-inch . Otterbox Defender Series Pro XT Best Rugged iPhone Duo Case Otterbox has a long history of producing sturdy smartphone cases. Although it might add a huge amount of heft and bulk to what is the thinnest iPhone Apple has ever made (when unfolded), it might be worth it, considering the price of the phone and its untested durability. This case has a raised lip around the outer display and a hinge guard that the company says lays flat – it looks like it means the hinge, not the phone itself – when the phone is open. You’ll pay for all that protection, though. Otterbox is charging $90 for the new case. It has no official release date, but presumably, it’ll come soon. For the more typical slab-style form factor phones, I’m more partial to Otterbox’s Commuter Series iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max cases, which offer beefy protection that’s not quite so unwieldy. Mous Ultra Thin Phone Case Best Thin iPhone Duo Case Maybe you just want to keep your iPhone Duo scratch-free; if that’s how you feel, Mous’s Ultra Thin Phone Case is a solid option. It’s made up of a rigid aramid fiber, and has a cover for the back of the phone, as well as a piece that hugs the outer edge of the front display. On the inside, the back cover has a microfiber layer, and sandwiched between the layers is a magnetic ring to ensure your phone can still support MagSafe wireless charging. The Mous Ultra Thin case costs about as much as the Duo case Apple makes, and it’ll still leave your phone’s hinge unprotected as that case appears to. But hey, as a fellow thin case liker, I get why you would make that compromise. Sometimes, a beefy case just makes your phone feel less cool. Spigen Ultra Hybrid Pro (Mag Fit) Best Clear iPhone Duo Case There aren’t a lot of clear cases yet for the iPhone Duo, at least not that I could see from case makers I tend to trust. Thankfully, Spigen is among those doing it, and its transparent Ultra Hybrid Pro (Mag Fit) has most of the things I’d want out of a clear case. It’s see-through all the way around, and features a magnetic ring for wirelessly charging your phone or popping MagSafe accessories like pop sockets and wallets on the back. One drawback, as I see it, could be the apparently bulbous hinge cover that probably keeps the Duo from laying flat when it’s all the way open. Another is its all-polycarbonate construction, which could make it a little overly rigid versus a hybrid case that uses flexible TPU as well. The company also offers one that’s similar to Dbrand’s Ghost Case, with opaque outer edges, while clear plastic makes up the back cover. The Spigen Ultra Hybrid Pro is priced at $60, which puts it at the lower end of many of the cases on this list. How to Pick an iPhone Duo Case I always recommend that prospective case buyers start by setting a budget for their new case – which might seem silly if you’re buying a $2,000 phone, but maybe that breaks the bank for you. Then figure out what you want the case to do. Is it purely for drop protection? Do you just want it to keep your phone from scratching? Does it need to be clear or opaque? Then, see what the manufacturers you’ve trusted in the past are doing. Something to additionally consider is that the iPhone Duo is a brand-new form factor, and Apple’s first go at the foldable market. The company is known for its patient, detail-driven approach to things, but despite the many leaks that seem to have predicted the Duo’s exact dimensions, there could still be quirks that case makers didn’t anticipate. As such I’d probably buy my first case straight from Apple, then wait to see how things shake out a few months down the line, after third-party manufacturers have been able to tweak their designs. I’d hate to drop my $2,000+ phone on the ground, only to watch the corner of my case pop off, leading to dings on the outer edge or worse, cracks on the screen itself. It’s not a bad idea to prioritize edge and hinge coverage, and keep in mind that many hinge covers can keep the phone from laying flat on its back when it’s unfolded all the way. Also keep in mind how the case looks on the phone and feels in your hand. Maybe you’re getting the ultimate in phone protection, a case that could let your phone survive being driven over by a tank, but is that really worth it if it ruins how it feels to use your device every day? Or if your super premium phone looks like it’s wrapped in one of those NERF iPad covers for kids?

items.title: Nintendo Was Reportedly Unhappy With Elon Musk's Saturday Night Live Wario Sketch
items.excerpt: Nintendo was reportedly unhappy with Elon Musk's 2021 Saturday Night Live sketch where he played Wario.
items.content_text: Nintendo was reportedly unhappy with Elon Musk's 2021 Saturday Night Live sketch where he played Wario. In 2021, Elon Musk starred in a Saturday Night Live sketch where he played Wario. The nefarious Nintendo character took the stand in a courtroom, where he was being accused of murdering everyone's favorite plumber, Mario. The skit was poorly received online and, apparently, by Nintendo itself. Kit Ellis and Krysta Yang, two former Nintendo PR managers, revealed in a recent episode of their YouTube show that the SNL skit "did not go well" with Nintendo at the time. The two got on the subject following the recent Saturday Night Live sketch where The Legend of Zelda protagonist Link and GTA 6's Jason Duvall debated each other over who would have the better game. The sketch largely pokes fun at The Legend of Zelda while trying to make GTA 6 seem like the "cooler" game, which itself led to some mixed reactions online. Nevertheless, Ellis and Yang think that it probably went over better than Musk's sketch. The two recalled being at Nintendo when the skit aired and stated that it was "not beloved." Ellis went on to note that the sketch was also oddly timed, as there wasn't even a new Wario game or product when it happened. He went on to say that the sketch also pushed into "uncomfortable" for Nintendo, likely referencing some of the more risque jokes in the skit. The SNL crew made jokes about Mario using cocaine, Luigi sleeping with Princess Peach, and featured a video of Luigi's censored penis. It was... interesting, to say the least. Naturally, it's understandable if Nintendo wasn't thrilled about its family-friendly characters being portrayed as sexual deviants. SNL has parodied Nintendo a number of other times, including a sketch featuring a dark and gritty version of Mario Kart , heavily inspired by HBO's adaptation of The Last of Us.
items.title_en: Nintendo Was Reportedly Unhappy With Elon Musk's Saturday Night Live Wario Sketch

items.title: Breaking Bad Star RJ Mitte Dead at 34
items.excerpt: RJ Mitte, the actor best known for playing Walter White Jr. in Breaking Bad, has died at 34.
items.content_text: RJ Mitte, the actor best known for playing Walter White Jr. in Breaking Bad, has died at 34. TMZ reported that a county official in Texas confirmed the news that he died today, October 12, 2026. The site stated it was told that Mitte died by suicide. Additional details surrounding his death are unclear. An investigation is ongoing. Mitte started his career in Hollywood with a small role in Disney's Hannah Montana before appearing as the son of Bryan Cranston's Walter White when Breaking Bad premiered in 2008. He played Walter 'Flynn' White Jr. for 56 episodes, cementing him not only as one of the AMC show's most prominent characters, but one of the more recognizable characters in TV history. Mitte appeared in all five seasons of Breaking Bad but went on to have an acting career that saw him contribute to different mediums across the entertainment spectrum. In 2013, he showed up in a music video for Steel Panther's "Party Like Tomorrow Is The End of the World." In 2014, he appeared in nine episodes of the television series Switched at Birth. While his time on TV screens saw him also play roles in things like Now Apocalypse and This Close, his movie resume included parts in things like 2021's Triumph, 2020's The Oak Room, and 2019's All the Little Things We Kill. His most recent project saw him star as Joshua in this year's Talking to Stranger. Representatives for Mitte shared a statement with TMZ confirming the passing. They called him a "beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate." "RJ Mitte was best known for his role as Walter 'Flynn' White Jr. on AMC’s critically acclaimed, award-winning series Breaking Bad," the message continued. "Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion. Beyond entertaining friends and family around the world, he served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s." Others are taking the time to remember his impact not only as an actor but also as an important disability rights advocate. items.title: The Tiny XTEINK X4 Pro Ebook Reader Is on Sale for Its Lowest-Ever Price
items.excerpt: The tiny XTEINK X4 Pro packs all the features you'd want in an ebook reader into an easily pocketable device, and it's on sale now at Amazon.
items.content_text: Our world is increasingly filled with colorful, glowing screens it can be hard to take your eyes off of. If you would like to decrease your screen time, you might also want to increase your reading time. One of the most convenient ways to do that is to use a tiny e-book reader like the XTEINK X4 Pro, currently on sale at Amazon for $84.15 (down from $99). It’s a limited-time deal, so it could vanish at any time. Let’s look at what this little device can do. XTEINK X4 Pro Is on Sale for $84 The XTEINK X4 Pro is a tiny, easily pocketable e-book reader; it's 5.95mm thin and weighs just 72 grams. The e-ink display measures 4.3 inches diagonally, which is big enough to read without straining your eyes. But the whole device is barely bigger than a credit card. It can even magnetically snap onto the back of your phone. It has most of the features you’d expect in an ebook reader in 2026. It has a dual-tone front light so you can read in low-light (or no-light) situations. The e-ink display is easy to read in direct sunlight, just like the pages of a paper book. It has both touchscreen and physical buttons to turn pages forward and back. And because e-ink displays require very little power, a single charge lasts weeks. Format-wise, it supports EPUB, TXT, MOBI, PDF formats. You can load books onto it using the official app, the cloud, or a microSD card. The app can even convert ebooks from different formats into a format viewable on the device. Included in the Box XTEINK X4 Pro Adhesive Metal Ring (x2) Screen Cleaning Kit Magnetic Charging Adapter Matte Screen Protector User Manual It has buttons for home, power on/off, next page, and previous page. It has a microSD card slot and a lanyard hole. It doesn’t come with a charging cable, but it does include an adapter that lets you use a USB-C charging cable to charge it using a magnet to attach it to your device. It also comes with a magnet ring you can stick to the back of the device to make it snap to the back of your phone. Once you go into the settings, you’ll find this thing is super customizable. You can change the functions of the buttons. You can adjust things like the font, line spacing, text size, and brightness. You can go into night mode, and even set a color temperature to trigger on and off automatically at certain times of day. Personally, I love reading paper books, but I have to admit they’re not the most convenient things in the world to haul around, especially if you don’t want to bring a bag where you’re going. Even a Kindle is too big to carry on your person. That’s where a device like this fits in, so you can carry a book (or folder full of books) with you wherever you go, even in the same pocket as your phone. I also like the small screen size, because it limits the number of words on a page. Sometimes, when I’m reading a textbook or a big hardcover, I find the wall of text on the page visually unappealing, especially if the print is small. I look at a page like that, and think, “I’m never going to read all that” – and I was an English major. On the XTEINK X4 Pro, you’ll never have an intimidating amount of text on the screen. The best part about it is the size. Because it's so pocketable, you can just bring it with you anywhere you go. Then, when you find yourself in a situation where you'd normally pull out your phone and start doomscrolling, you can pull out the X4 Pro instead and read a few pages in whatever book you're currently reading.

items.title: TCL 27C2A Pro Review
items.excerpt: The TCL 272A Pro can impress in testing, but in practice its shortcomings become all the more apparent and it fails to shine nearly as brightly.
items.content_text: The TCL 27C2A Pro is a Mini LED gaming monitor geared to compete with some of the hottest 4K gaming monitors on the market. It offers a 4K panel with quantum dot pixels and a dual-mode that can trade off resolution for speed, much like some other high-end monitors. The TCL 27C2A Pro promises a lot, but its $999 price tag raises a lot of questions. Design and Features The TCL 27C2A Pro is a fairly tame monitor with a white-and-black color scheme that seems to chase after either Alienware’s or Samsung’s approval. Other than some RGB lighting, it’s not terribly gaudy, but it’s not incredibly pretty either. The display squeezes in a 27-inch 4K panel that runs at 160Hz in its native mode or 320Hz when swapped down to 1080p. This kind of dual-mode technology has been popping up on more and more 4K monitors, and it’s great to see as it gives them more flexibility to serve as platforms for AAA titles with gorgeous graphical assets as well as competitive esports games where speed is almost all that matters. The panel features quantum dots and Mini LED backlighting with over 2,300 dimming zones (2,304 to be exact). That gives it a rated 98% coverage of the DCI-P3 color space and rated peak brightness of 2,000 nits — more on that later. The TCL 27C2A Pro might have a $999 MSRP, but little about the monitor’s constructions feels like it ever should have. It builds on the earlier 27C2A non-pro model, which was cheaper and had fewer dimming zones and a lower peak brightness. But that this more expensive model was built on the bones of a cheap display makes it feel cheap as a result. The stand and back of the monitor are covered in flimsy plastic. Though, TCL includes some colorful and modestly bright RGB lighting on the back of the monitor that at least makes it look more fun. The monitor has an adjustable stand that gives you all the height, swivel, tilt, and rotational adjustment you’d expect from a high-end monitor, but it’s terribly jiggly. Any motion to my task transmits up through the stand. Thankfully, the monitor can be placed on a VESA mount. Rather than having a sturdy, rigid hole through the stand for cable routing, the back of the stand has a little rubber strap that slides down to form a small loop that the cables can go through, but they don’t end up looking super tidy in practice. The monitor also uses an external power brick that you’ll need to find space for on or under your desk. The monitor gets a couple things right in its design, at least. It includes DisplayPort and two HDMI ports. It also offers a USB-C connection that can handle video input and up to 90W of power output to a connected device. All of the ports can work with the display’s 4K/160Hz peak, though you’ll want to make sure you have cables that can do the job too. The monitor uses a joystick for controls, which makes navigation easy. The joystick sits front and center underneath the display, so it’s easy to reach. The TCL 27C2A Pro also includes speakers, but that should be a given in any monitor this expensive. This ensures you always have an option for audio output even when you don’t have headphones or dedicated speakers handy, so it’s a plus. Gaming and Performance The TCL 27C2A Pro is a decent monitor for gaming, but it fails to punch up into greatness. It’s sharp and smooth, but not sharper or smoother than others on the block. Its ability to go bright can be handy, especially with its decent anti-glare qualities, but that’s about where its lead ends. Even then, sometimes the monitor just wants to go too dark. When I tried to watch Dune, every dark scene just sank into too much darkness, leaving it hard to see anything despite the monitor’s very bright capabilities. The same happened while watching Avatar 2, with most of the movie bright and lovely but the final night of action growing incredibly dim. A few hours of Assassin’s Creed Shadows went well enough, but when I accidentally took out all the lights in a tower while fighting, suddenly I could hardly see what was on screen to make it through the combat. With local dimming, small bright elements can just about vanish on the display, too. My mouse cursor moving across a black screen dims considerably, and starfields look awful. The TCL 27C2A Pro hits its stride when displaying bright and colorful content. Hades 2 sings, rendered in sharp fidelity and running smoothly. There’s not enough ghosting to be a bother in this game, and the color simply glows out of the monitor. There’s still some annoying artifacts from local dimming, such as certain elements (like the coin counter) appearing dim when it’s in an otherwise dark section of the screen, but these are generally subtle and hard to notice. As things turn darker or rely more on contrast for effect, the MiniLED tech’s shortcomings next to OLED become obvious. In areas of strong contrast, such as a black and white box next to each other, exhibit a haze where the local dimming overlaps with one of the areas, dimming a portion of what should be bright white. White text on a black background can appear dim and unevenly lit. That’s rough for captions. In bright scenes, the Mini LED backlighting can definitely deliver, but black pixels close to bright elements get lifted so the actual contrast in that area will fall back to typical IPS levels. In the end, the visual quality is simply too situational. Next to an OLED display, the differences really stand out. The whole image on the TCL 27C2A Pro is simply flattened. Little details that pop on OLED don’t have that effect on the TCL 27C2A Pro in many cases, and it’s because the contrast is neutered right where a detail should be emphasized because of the light doing the popping. This can leave things simply looking a little washed out. Then there’s the matter of the dual-mode settings. The 4K/160Hz mode looks good, but the monitor can drop down to 1080p/320Hz for faster visuals. I saw this type of tech in action on the Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM , and it worked quite well there. Going down in resolution that much is always going to hurt a little, but the TCL 27C2A Pro looked particularly soft, with even decently sized text almost appearing blurry. It wasn’t too dramatic in the throes of battle in Hades 2, but when stopping to enjoy the scenery or read dialogue, it was more of a bother. The TCL 27C2A Pro is capable of putting up some terribly impressive numbers when tested with a colorimeter, though. I measured its color gamut at 100% of the sRGB and 99% of the DCI-P3 color spaces. That’s just what you should expect from quantum dot color. The monitor defaults to 50% brightness, which hits a modest 167.8 nits, but if you dial it up to max brightness, it soars up to 570 nits. The wide color gamut and brightness don’t guarantee excellent visual performance in all conditions, though. At full brightness, it achieved a 5,930:1 contrast ratio, which sounds great on paper, but the use of local dimming zones, even if there are over 2,300 of them, means the contrast depends in part on where it’s being measured. A subsequent test saw the monitor reach 8,150:1 likely due simply to a small shift in colorimeter placement. With bright squares in each corner, I even measured perfect black at the center of the display, giving it infinite contrast. But if I move the colorimeter closer to the corners, suddenly black pixels can have a few tenths of a nit bleeding through. With a 6x4 checkboard, the monitor manages a much tamer 2,038:1 contrast ratio with HDR white measuring at 693 nits and black measuring at 0.34 nits. HDR has a lot of benefits for the monitor. It continues to cover the broad 99% coverage of the DCI-P3 colorspace alongside a comfortable 6500K whitepoint, and it can simply blast light out of a big enough area. Both a 10% window and a full white screen hit a little over 2,000 nits. That’s where its edge over OLED lies, as OLED monitors are lucky to hit half that for a 10% window and a quarter of that for a full white screen. Even a 1% window hit 975 nits. That said, smaller HDR highlights (e.g., muzzle flares or stars) will either lack brightness or lift the brightness of surrounding pixels. The speakers on the monitor are kind of boxy and unpleasant. They put out respectable volume for casual listening, but won’t sound great for music or games, especially where spatial sound is concerned. After gaming on them for a while, they really started to grate on my ears. So, trust me, use a gaming headset. Purchasing guide TCL lists the 27C2A Pro at $999 on Amazon , which is frankly too much. The monitor does go on sale occasionally, though, so you should be able to get it much cheaper. And, really, you shouldn't get it unless you can get a hefty discount.
items.title_en: TCL 27C2A Pro Review

items.title: Student Suspended After Teachers Discover Death Note Notebook, Sparking Police Investigation
items.excerpt: A student at a Massachusetts middle school found herself at the center of a police investigation after administrators discovered her Death Note notebook.
items.content_text: A student at a Massachusetts middle school found herself at the center of a police investigation after administrators discovered her Death Note notebook. The incident took place at Chocksett Middle School in Sterling, Massachusetts. Students had already left for the day when staff discovered the notebook at around 4pm on September 30. Police and school officials then conducted an investigation, interviewing both its owner and other students, and quickly determined that the Death Note — which contained a few names of its owner’s classmates — did not pose a legitimate threat. However, the student was suspended for three days. “When we spoke with the student, the student explained that the notebook was connected to an anime television series and was not intended as a threat,” principal Tina Boss wrote in a letter addressed to the school’s community, adding that there was “no indication that the notebook or its contents were intended as a threat toward the school or any particular student.” “Based on the information available at this time, the Sterling Police Department is not seeking criminal charges in connection with this incident,” the Sterling Police Department said in a press release. Despite coming to this conclusion, police stood watch on the school grounds Tuesday, October 6, with officials saying it "will maintain a presence as it sees appropriate," as reported by local news outlet Boston.com . A Death Note , in the anime of the same name, is a supernatural notebook owned by gods of death called shinigami. If someone writes the name of another person in the notebook, they will die. There are a few other rules , but that’s basically the gist of it. Death Notes are often sold as merchandise for fans of the anime and manga series as basic notebooks with the 'Death Note' lettering on the front cover — but given the state of things in the United States over the last decade, it makes sense why parents and school administrators would be concerned for students’ safety after finding such a notebook. A mother of one of the children whose name was written in this particular Death Note expressed frustration with how the situation was handled on social media. “A student who created a kill list with our daughter’s name on it is being allowed to return after just a three-day suspension… to the same classroom, within feet of her every day!” she wrote in a post on Facebook. “Yes, a safety plan is in place. But how does that plan give my daughter peace of mind when she still has to sit in the same classroom as the student who put her name on that list? She deserves to feel safe in her classroom, every single day.” This isn’t the first time a student’s Death Note notebook has prompted such a reaction after being discovered at school; in September 2024, teachers at an I Promise school in Akron, Ohio were alerted after a student’s homemade ‘Death Note,’ written on sheets of loose leaf paper, was found. Although nothing came of the situation, parents of students whose names were written in the notebook similarly expressed dissatisfaction at how things were handled.

This new installment brings the racing action to Japan, in the series’ largest map to date, with all sorts of biomes to explore, ranging from mountaintops to Tokyo streets, and over 550 vehicles to do it in. We gave this game a 10/10 in our review , and the PS5 version promises to be just as good. Read on for details. items.title: Epic Reportedly Pushing Devs to Use AI, Delays Secret Star Wars and Marvel Crossover Shooter
items.excerpt: Epic Games has reportedly delayed its secret Star Wars and Marvel crossover shooter as it pushes its developers to shift to an "AI first" production model.
items.content_text: Epic Games has reportedly delayed its secret Star Wars and Marvel crossover shooter as it pushes its developers to shift to an "AI first" production model. Details on the yet-to-be-announced Disney video game were shared by Bloomberg today. The site's report stated the untitled crossover experience was slated for release in March, but has since been pushed back to accommodate a new internal release plan that has yet to be shared. Epic developers attached to the project have reportedly been encouraged to use tools such as Anthropic's AI assistant, Claude, with humans expected to oversee that work. Bloomberg also obtained an internal message shared by one of the Star Wars/Marvel game's directors. "No more hand-written code,” an excerpt from the message said. The same message is then said to have added that all art for the project would be "generated with full AI workflows." The report continued, stating that Epic underestimated the time and resources necessary to develop the Star Wars and Marvel shooter. Progress has been slower than expected, leading to the delay. When and where it will launch is unclear. "We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do," Epic communications director Jake Jones told Bloomberg in a statement. The site added that Epic's push for what appears to be a project that leans heavily on AI left many of its developers "stunned." News of the Star Wars and Marvel shooter's schedule change follows another Bloomberg report from earlier this year, which stated that Epic was working on an extraction shooter featuring Disney characters . It was said to be similar to Embark Studios' Arc Raiders at the time. Just moments before news of Epic's AI push broke, studio founder and CEO Tim Sweeney published a post on X/Twitter saying that the studio has a "huge pivot underway." He added that they are "moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration." "The aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people," he continued, "but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal." In a follow-up post, Sweeney said , "Our more modest aim is to survive the AI revolution, help other developers do the same, and come out on the other end making better code and content faster." "The biggest change will be much faster time from having an idea to playtesting it," he said in another post. "This will be great for gameplay, as most of the recent AAA failures can be attributed to game systems going through far too much of their development process without being able to playtest." Disney purchased a $1.5 billion stake in the Fortnite developer in 2024 in a move that cemented their relationship at the time. Outside of more crossovers within Epic's still-popular battle royale-centered video game, it seems we've yet to see the extent of their collaborations. Meanwhile, Disney recently refuted claims that it was interested in outright acquiring the game studio .

items.title: Every Magic: The Gathering Set Confirmed for 2027, Including Marvel: Darkhold Destiny
items.excerpt: Wizards of the Coast is scaling back to six Magic: The Gathering sets in 2027. Here is the full schedule, including Kamigawa, Zhalfir, and what we could expect from Universes Beyond
items.content_text: So much has been made of Universes Beyond, Magic: The Gathering’s crossovers with other IP, that many have dubbed the game “the Fortnite of card games”. 2026 saw seven sets in a single calendar year, which means that—at the time of writing—we’re closing in on November's release of Star Trek. In 2027, though, things are changing — not only is Wizards of the Coast cutting the number of sets down to six (with three Universes Within and three Universes Beyond), but we won’t get a back-to-back of Universes Beyond at all. Hooray! Here’s all we know about Magic’s 2027 sets so far, and what to expect from them, including the recently revealed Marvel: Darkhold Destiny . Nauctis: The Sunken Realm February 5, 2027 The first set of 2027 will debut in early February, and it’ll take us to Nauctis. This “Sunken Realm” is all about being under the waves, so you can expect some deep-sea humans alongside merfolk, homarids, and seals. Here’s Wizards of the Coast’s synopsis: “As tensions bubble between two warring kingdoms, a group of unlikely heroes must rise to the occasion—or their home will be swallowed up by the abyssal depths of the ocean. Adventures await under the water, and players will come face to face with fearsome creatures that dwell far, far from the surface.” Marvel: Darkhold Destiny April 9, 2027 We knew we'd be getting more Marvel sets, but we didn't quite expect the spooky Darkhold Destiny to arrive before something like the X-Men. Still, this time things are a little different: This is based on an original story, rather than just dragging Marvel characters into Magic. Expect four Commander Decks, two Scene Boxes, Play Boosters, Bundles, and yes, those all-important Collector Boosters. Kamigawa: Titanbreach June 4, 2027 2026 saw two trips back to iconic planes with Lorwyn and Strixhaven, and in 2027 we’re heading back to Kamigawa. The cyberpunk-infused setting will see a huge shift when the Ikoria plane crashes into it, leading to a mechs versus kaiju set. “Return to Kamigawa and harness the power of next-generation mechs that can match the might of any titan. The Kamigawans will need all the help they can get, because the behemoths of Ikoria may be the greatest threat this plane has ever seen.” “And if you'd rather be the monster than fight them, you can harness your favorite creatures from Ikoria in the battle for the city. Suit up, get ready to rumble, and witness a battle on a scale you've never seen before.” Zhalfir October 1, 2027 Zhalfir sounds a lot like it’ll be a love letter to longtime Magic fans, arriving as its own plane and bringing back the legendary chronomancer, Teferi Akosa. It’ll lean into the afrofantasy subgenre, but we don’t know much else about it just yet. “Immerse yourself in the beauty of Zhalfir and harness innovative new forms of magic. The minds behind this plane have crafted some especially mind-bending cards, each embracing the unique visual design of Magic's take on the afrofantasy genre.” “And because Zhalfir is so closely tied to an era of Magic that many players hold dear, we're honoring its legacy in every aspect of the set. This is Magic: The Gathering as you remember it, crafted with the love and care of our contemporary design philosophy.” Universes Beyond We are yet to have anything confirmed for 2027 Universes Beyond beyond the new Marvel Darkhold Destiny set, but that won't stop us speculating on what could be in store. For now, we have the dates in which we should expect the three sets. August 6, 2027 November 19, 2027 Beyond that, if you'll pardon the pun, the only piece of info we have is from Hasbro CEO Chris Cocks notes in the recent earnings report . Cocks noted feedback on recent Universes Beyond sets, which have run the gamut from two trips to Middle-Earth, just as many visits to New York City, every single Final Fantasy, and, soon, Star Trek. “The one thing I'll say on the Universes Beyond partners that we have next year is they'll probably be a bit more fantasy-adjacent," he explained. "And I don't think any of them will take place in New York City because we definitely have gotten that feedback from some fans." From that, there are a lot of potential crossovers that would be fun for Magic: The Gathering, but the idea of refocusing on fantasy IP certainly is interesting. We've recently predicted it could be anything from Games of Thrones, to Elden Ring, Warhammer: Age of Sigmar, The Legend of Zelda, The Witcher, or World of Warcraft. But, that's purely speculation, and we shall have to wait and see what is officially announced later this year. Lloyd Coombes is an experienced freelancer in tech, gaming and fitness seen at Polygon, Eurogamer, Macworld, TechRadar and many more. He's a big fan of Magic: The Gathering and other collectible card games, much to his wife's dismay.

items.title: Gears of War: E-Day Review
items.excerpt: A prequel that returns to the heart of this series.
items.content_text: To the casual observer, Gears of War has always been a heavy-metal third-person cover shooter about a bunch of meatheads with chainsaws attached to their guns fighting aliens. But what Gears fans know all too well is that the real secret to the series’s two decades of success isn’t the killer graphics, the smart cover mechanics, or the gloriously gratuitous gore – although those things are all certainly significant parts of the recipe. It’s the heart. Marcus and Dom’s brotherhood. JD or Del’s sacrifice (depending on what you chose to do in Gears 5). Dom’s relentless love for Maria. And so my biggest question heading into Gears of War: E-Day, a prequel to the first game set 14 years prior on the day the Locust emerged from underneath the planet Sera, was how it would hang onto that heart when we already knew our armor-clad bros would definitely be alive by the end. I’m thrilled to say that E-Day carries its own satisfying emotional weight, with additional welcomed backstory for Marcus and Dom leading the way – oh, and the action is pretty top-notch, too. E-Day begins with our Coalition of Ordered Government (COG) heroes, Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago, completing a ceremonial tour to honor their service in the finally-ended 79-year Pendulum Wars. We get glimpses of how each of them is reckoning with the end of the only thing they’ve ever known: Marcus is ready to re-enlist and hoping Dom will join him, while Dom is ready to go home to his wife Maria and their two young children, who are growing up without him. Of course, things quickly go to Hell – or rather, Hell comes up to them. Gears of War: E-Day does an excellent job of conveying both the uncertainty and the horror of what’s happening to these characters, even when we as players know exactly what’s going on. What I said about the Gears 5 (2019) It’s not surprising at all that Gears 5 is an excellent third-person action game. This iconic series has never really had a misfire, even when changing hands from original developer Epic to The Coalition, and the hot streak remains unbroken. What was unexpected is just how effectively it doubles down on story with a character-focused, consequence-filled tale that plays to one of the franchise’s most underappreciated strengths and backs it up with fun, welcome additions to both its gameplay formula and flow. And that’s just the campaign: add in a heavy-hitting multiplayer lineup of Versus, Versus Arcade, Horde, and Escape and it makes Gears 5 one of the best and most versatile action-game packages in recent memory. - Ryan McCaffrey, September 13, 2019 Score: 9 Read the full Gears 5 review . By happenstance, Marcus and Dom get unofficially paired up with ex-Gear Mags Carter and rookie Gear Lucas Reyes, who happen to be at the same bar when the Locust tremors begin, before the quartet officially becomes Bravo Squad once the COG starts organizing its defenses. E-Day deserves a lot of credit here: In a prequel like this where you’re already attached to the leads, it would be easy for Carter and Reyes to be throwaway side characters who exist only to further the stories of our two well-known heroes. But E-Day makes time for your lesser-known Bravo squadmates, dedicating entire meaningful and enjoyable sections to establishing them in this world and getting you to care about them. The unfolding nightmare of E-Day is reflected in both the types of Locust monsters you face as the campaign progresses as well as the sorts of weapons you’ll need to put them back in the ground. Easily-dispatched Wretches and run-of-the-mill, Hammerburst-wielding Drones are on the front lines as Bravo Squad wonders what the hell it’s up against in the invasion’s opening hours. You’ll take them down with Gears of War staples like the Gnasher shotgun and Lancer, both the bayonet-clad original version and the prototype of the chainsaw-equipped revision. Yes, you’ll get your hands on Gears’s most famous firearm pretty early, and you even get to witness its fun little origin story. E-Day makes time for your lesser-known squadmates and gets you to care. But as you move through the first hours of the Locust invasion, Bravo Squad is continually confused and terrified at the increasingly deadly horrors trying to kill them. The monster menagerie is, naturally, a mix of foes you have and haven’t seen before in other Gears of War games, and the battles get steadily more white-knuckle as you make your way through the five-act story. Giant, frog-like hopping freaks that arc multi-gallon acidic loogies at you. Heavies that come in multiple varieties, most menacingly the one that fires a medium-range Gorehook – a hook on a chain that will typically down you in one hit. On that note, one of my few complaints about Gears of War: E-Day is related to the down-but-not-out situations you’ll find yourself in throughout the campaign. When, not if, you get downed, your allies will occasionally be standing right next to you and not revive you. In fairness, it wasn’t a constant occurrence, but there were numerous times throughout my 15-18 hour first playthrough when I got stomped to death by a Locust heavy because one of my buddies either stood next to me and didn’t get me up, ran off and left me for dead, or never even got over to me as I mashed the X button to cling to life for a while. The immediate solution for this is to play through E-Day in four-player online co-op (two-player split-screen is the limit on a single Xbox), but I sure hope a patch resolves this inconsistent AI behavior sooner rather than later as well. Guns Aplenty As with the Locust enemies, E-Day’s weapons are a mix of old and new, and my goodness do I love them. Every weapon has a unique purpose to suit a particular combat strategy. And man, it still feels awesome to blast a Locust Heavy to bits with the Gnasher shotgun, cut a Drone into pieces with the Lancer Prototype’s chainsaw attachment, or explode a Locust sniper’s head with a scoped-Longshot kill. But there’s so much more in there beyond those Gears classics. The Breechshot, first introduced in the often-forgotten Gears of War: Judgment, ended up being one of my go-tos the longer the campaign went on, as it offered solid range and stopping power without being as cumbersome as something like the Longshot sniper rifle. But there are a lot of weapons I’d give shoutouts to as well, like the Incinerator, which shotgun-blasts a burst of flesh-melting Imulsion; the Ripper, which is basically the Gears-universe equivalent of a SAW; and the ol’ favorite Torque Bow, which has a hell of a windup but then unleashes an explosive arrow at your target. I loved the weapon complement here, as well as the options that deep roster of firearms afforded me in some of the campaign’s later battles. And it’s not just that all of these weapons are fun to use in the right situation. They can also all be modified and upgraded through E-Day’s new Weapon Mod and Tactical Gear system. You’ll encounter dozens of yellow Hard Cases lightly hidden throughout the world for you to find. Each contains a mod for one weapon or another, such as accuracy enhancers, scopes, or clip extenders. Completing optional secondary objectives around the major industrial city of Kalona where E-Day takes place also grants these same rewards. Each weapon has four mod slots, which you’ll unlock as you go, and I found myself constantly tweaking each weapon to find the right mix of add-ons that suited my playstyle. As such, I was plenty motivated to find every Hard Case I could and complete every secondary objective possible. In addition to this is the Tactical Gear that modifies your armor, giving you your choice of a few squad-affecting special abilities that recharge on a cooldown timer after you use them. Again, you’ll unlock more as you progress, but once I got my hands on the Stim that allowed me to heal myself and any teammates within its radius for a short time, I was never tempted by any of the other choices. All of these customization options evolve the classic Gears of War combat in a welcome but not radical way that I appreciate, while liberally placed Supply Caches let you cycle weapons and mods rather frequently if you so choose. And you’ll be glad for the ability to rearrange your weapon loadout often in E-Day’s mini-boss fights and full-blown boss battles. Almost all of them are memorable in a good way. With, again, a mix of old and new “faces,” these were often barely-scrape-by bouts during my playthrough and ones I welcomed both when they arrived and when I emerged victorious. Almost all of the boss fights are memorable in a good way. E-Day is packed with beautiful locations. The destroyed downtown of Kalona; the pitch-black, Locust-dug caves underneath it; the almost sinister-looking Imulsion refinery; the peaceful mountaintops outside the city. Although the entire campaign doesn’t take place there, you’ll spend a healthy amount of time in Kalona, and the massive but dense battle spaces there are an excellent evolution of the mostly empty open-world areas from Gears 5. The freedom feels far more organic and meaningful here, as there are so many interesting things around almost every corner. In addition to the aforementioned secondary objectives that grant meaningful Weapon Mod upgrades, there are hidden objects with optionally-viewed details that add a bit of color to a world in the process of recovering from a 79-year civil war, only to be invaded and destroyed by the Locust in a few days. The gorgeous visuals are brought down only by infrequent but noticeable framerate hitches, even while playing in Performance Mode on the Xbox Series X. As such, I can’t recommend playing on the 30fps Quality Mode – at least not before a patch or two. On a side note, I appreciate that E-Day doesn’t do the all-too-common “make the player run the gauntlet of everything they’ve already fought, but multiply it” endgame sequence. Instead, your mettle is tested plenty of times along the way, with ample quiet moments to punctuate the loud action. And the ending is, I’ll say without spoiling anything, satisfying , which isn’t an easy thing to pull off when, as I mentioned, we already know that Marcus and Dom make it out of E-Day alive. And thank goodness, because I need more quippy Marcus Fenix one-liners in my life; I can’t get enough of them. Multiplayer Impressions With Gears of War: E-Day officially launched and live servers hosting multiplayer matches for about a week now, I’ve spent a good bit of time with each of E-Day’s online modes – though I’d already spent some initial time with Horde Siege in the beta weekends prior to launch. Horde Siege is what I want to talk about most, because I think it’s the tastiest dish on this prequel’s multiplayer menu, but I’ll first address the ol’ standby: Versus mode, aka the only multiplayer mode that’s been there since the very beginning. Versus is, for better and for worse, a Gnasher shotgun wall-bounce-fest. As it always has been. There is a flow state you can achieve in it that’s just delightful. The Warpath mode helps keep things moving, with each team trying to secure and maintain control of rotating zones. It’s nothing we haven’t seen a hundred times before, but it works. It draws all of the action to one place, and Gears of War has always thrived in closer-quarters combat (no disrespect to the ace Longshot snipers out there). I never had trouble finding a match, and crossplay is enabled straight away. There’s also no shortage of items to unlock the longer you play, so you’ve got incentives to stay on the hamster wheel match after match, day after day. While you can bring your four-person squad of friends into matchmaking and stick together round after round, E-Day unfortunately lacks private matches entirely. That is a disappointment, because if you’ve got a big group of friends who just want to face off against each other for a night of fun, it’s not going to happen barring a successful low-odds diceroll. E-Day does get points for allowing you (and your friends, if you like) to play against bots, though, if you’d rather eliminate the human element entirely. And laudably, those bots can be set to any difficulty level, so there’s fun to be had here whether you’re completely new to Gears or a 20-year veteran of the series seeking the highest challenge. Horde Siege, meanwhile, is the star of the show. Heck, Gears of War arguably started (or at least popularized) the PvE trend with Horde’s debut in Gears of War 2. Horde Siege comes in many flavors, including an onboarding option for new players, a limited-time mission that I look forward to seeing future iterations of, shorter Blitz campaigns, standard Siege runs, and full-blown old-school Horde. Maps are sliced from the huge city of Kalona in the single-player campaign, so if you’ve completed it you’ll already be right at home. What’s really cool is that three other four-person squads are running around the same massive maps you are, and they’re each fighting their own battles. It doesn’t suddenly turn Gears into a PvE version of battle royale or anything quite on that scale, but it does make matches feel a little more alive when you see another group trying to beat back a big Brumak in the distance while you’re trying to exfil on your King Raven helicopter. The Horde Siege mode is the star of the multiplayer show. In terms of moment-to-moment gameplay, I really like how random, optional secondary tasks will pop up between your main Horde Siege objectives, and completing them nets rewards like lowering the costs of upgrades between rounds. And yes, the Supply Caches are just as critical in Horde Siege as they are in the campaign. More so, probably. Killing Locust and successfully achieving objectives nets you points to spend on ammo refills, defensive items (which you will 100% need!) like Mortar Sentries and Spike Traps, and more. Furthermore, there is very much a meta progression built into Horde Siege mode as well. It’s class-based, taking the campaign’s Tactical Gear,Armor Mods, and cooldown-timed powerups and divvying them up into Assault, Breacher, Marksman, and Medic classes. I opted to stick with the Medic, which was the same kit I used in the campaign, as I preferred being able to heal and revive myself and my teammates in tough spots. And oh man, there are plenty of tough spots. I rarely encountered a calm moment when playing Horde Siege, especially after completing the first couple of objectives. Things get spicy in a hurry. My teammates and I frequently found ourselves under heavy pressure on all sides from crazy combinations of bad guys, like Heavy Boomers and Reavers, Heavies with Gorehooks and a Brumak, and those damn floating hot-air balloon-looking bastards with the last damn boss of the game. And that’s to say nothing of the e-holes constantly popping up and spewing more enemies out of the ground at you. Needless to say, working together is clutch, but surviving and thriving is a blast. I absolutely love what Horde has evolved into with Horde Siege.

items.title: Marvel's VisionQuest Episodes 1 & 2 Review (No Spoilers)
items.excerpt: VisionQuest may struggle a bit to reestablish the titular hero in this post-WandaVision MCU, but at least the series has James Spader’s Ultron to fall back upon. Read our spoiler-free review of the first two episodes.
items.content_text: The first two episodes of Marvel’s VisionQuest debut on Disney+ on Wednesday, October 14. One of the most frustrating things about the post-Endgame MCU is how long it takes Marvel to circle back around and follow up on loose ends. Heck, they waited five years between Spider-Man sequels. And that’s to say nothing of the numerous post-credits scenes that still remain unresolved . VisionQuest is yet one more example of Marvel taking its sweet time to address a character who’s been trapped in storytelling limbo. Five years after WandaVision wrapped, we finally have a series dealing with the fate of Paul Bettany’s White Vision. But it’s not necessarily Vision himself who emerges as the beating heart of the series. WandaVision is essentially the final leg of the trilogy begun by WandaVision in 2021 and continued by Agatha All Along in 2024 . When last we saw Bettany’s characters in the WandaVision finale, the regular Vision returned to blissful oblivion, while his emotionless clone fled Westview to ponder his own existence. Half a decade later, he’s still very much in the pondering phase. By day, works in a bar and struggles to master the nuances of human interaction. By night, he literally lives inside his own head in a fanciful construct populated by the various other Tony Stark-designed AI units. He’s a being who barely exists in the physical world any longer, until circumstances arise that force him back into action. To be frank, as much as Bettany’s Vision is one of the best and most nuanced MCU characters, the series is a bit of a tough sell out of the gate. For one thing, the idyllic mansion construct feels like a rote, poor man’s recreation of what WandaVision was doing all those years ago, only without the TV sitcom conceit. It also feels like an attempted nod towards Tom King and Gabriel Hernandez Walta’s incredible 2015 Vision comic, though only in the most superficial sense. The production design in these scenes can't really be faulted, but there's nothing that WandaVision or Loki didn't do better in that regard. On a deeper level, Vision is not at all the same character we’ve known and loved for the past 11 years. The old Vision, despite being a synthetic lifeform, was by far the most human and compassionate of the Avengers. He was responsible for some of the most poignant lines in the MCU. This new Vision utterly lacks that charm. He’s cold and distant. He doesn’t understand humans, much less feel any appreciation for their struggles and foibles. That’s the entire point of the series - the question of whether this carbon copy can gain the insight and emotional maturity that his predecessor possessed. Now it’s Ultron who has something to teach Vision about the plight and beauty of mankind. Regardless, this newer, less compassionate Vision is a harder character to connect with. Bettany certainly draws a firm distinction between the roles in his performance, but there’s just something a little off-putting about a Vision who shows such contempt for his fellow man and kills with abandon. By the end of Episode 2, that problem begins to recede somewhat, but there’s definitely a major adjustment period fans of the character will have to endure. Luckily, if the series struggles to make its central protagonist fully resonate with viewers, it has a solid supporting cast to fall back upon. It’s a lot of fun seeing the various AI entities given “human” form inside Vision’s mind. That includes F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), and, best of all, the return of Agent Carter’s James D’Arcy to the J.A.R.V.I.S. role. Each character has been tasked with helping Vision understand humanity in one way or another, and all serve as entertaining foils to our dour hero. Then there’s the real highlight of the series in Episodes 1 and 2, James Spader’s Ultron. Say what you will about 2015’s Avengers: Age of Ultron, but Spader was an inspired casting choice, and this series promises to finally realize the lingering, untapped potential of that character in the MCU. Ultron is neither entirely friend nor foe to Vision, but more a cranky, supremely bored prisoner left over from a bygone era. Spader plays the role with gusto, bringing even more gravelly, affected charm to an AI who believes himself to be the smartest guy in every room. These episodes make the most of the role reversal, as now it’s Ultron who has something to teach Vision about the plight and beauty of mankind. If it’s tough to fully connect with Vision out of the gate, Ultron alone makes the series worth watching. That’s not to say the series is devoid of any compelling human characters. Much as Agatha All Along marked the debut of the reincarnated Billy Maximoff (Joe Locke), VisionQuest focuses a great deal of attention on his brother Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) and his own struggle to understand his existence and reconcile two very different sets of memories. Tommy makes for a compelling secondary protagonist in Episode 2, and its his presence that finally forces Vision to start coming out of his vibranium shell a bit. On the villain front, these two episodes introduce us to Paladin (Todd Stashwick) and his handler (Diane Morgan). These two make for a fun pair, despite the fact that all of their interaction happens over the phone. In general, Stashwick brings plenty of campy energy to the screen, while at the same time molding his character into someone who feels like a legitimate threat to Vision despite the latter’s vastly superior powerset and refusal to engage in mind games.
